title: Episode 326: George III (Part 1): The American Revolution, the Loss of the Thirteen Colonies, and William Pitt the Younger
description:
The monumental early reign of King George III, the third Hanoverian monarch. Ascending the throne at twenty-two in 1760 proudly declaring he 'gloried in the name of Briton', George was moral, devoted to agriculture as 'Farmer George', and deeply faithful to his wife Queen Charlotte. Determined to reassert royal authority, George's insistence that Parliament had the right to tax American colonists sparked the Stamp Act crisis, the Boston Tea Party, and the American Revolutionary War. Rejecting the Olive Branch Petition, George witnessed the loss of the Thirteen Colonies in 1783, gracefully receiving John Adams as the first American ambassador. Forming an alliance with twenty-four-year-old William Pitt the Younger, discover the complex sovereign at the crossroads of American independence.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series begins a grand two-part chronicle of Britain's longest-reigning king: a monarch of deep moral integrity who lost America, yet guided Britain to global triumph: King George III. Here is George with part one: the American Revolution and William Pitt.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'I GLORY IN THE NAME OF BRITON': ACCESSION AND MARRIAGE: 1738 TO 1761
Born in June 1738 at Norfolk House in London, two months premature, George William Frederick was the first Hanoverian monarch born in Britain and speaking English without a German accent. Raised in strict, sheltered seclusion at Kew and Leicester House following the sudden death of his father, Frederick, Prince of Wales, young George was tutored by John Stuart, Earl of Bute, who instilled in the impressionable prince an exalted view of royal duty and high moral probity. Ascending the throne in October 1760 at age twenty-two, George made his historic declaration to Parliament: 'Born and educated in this country, I glory in the name of Briton!' In September 1761, George married seventeen-year-old Princess Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, whom he met for the first time on their wedding day. The marriage was remarkably happy, loving, and moral: George never took a mistress, fathering fifteen children with Charlotte. In 1762, George purchased Buckingham House—later Buckingham Palace—as a private family retreat for his queen. George III's childhood was overshadowed by the early death of his father Frederick, Prince of Wales, who died after being struck by a cricket ball. His mother Augusta, Princess of Wales, raised the young prince under strict moral vigilance at Kew, constantly urging him: 'George, be a king!' George took this paternal advice to heart: he was determined to free the monarchy from the corrupt Whig aristocratic oligarchs who had dominated his grandfather. His meeting with Princess Charlotte at St. James's Palace on their wedding day in September 1761 was a charming moment: when the seventeen-year-old German princess fell to her knees before him, George gently raised her up, embraced her, and won her lifelong love, creating a royal household of exemplary moral virtue.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: 'FARMER GEORGE': ROYAL SCIENCE AND AGRICULTURE
In an era of aristocratic debauchery, King George III was an exemplar of bourgeois domesticity, temperance, and intellectual curiosity. He rose at six in the morning, lit his own fires, dined on plain boiled mutton and turnips, and drank only barley water. He was an ardent patron of science and learning: he commissioned Sir William Herschel to construct a forty-foot reflecting telescope at Slough, leading to Herschel's discovery of the planet Uranus, which Herschel originally named Georgium Sidus—'George's Star'—in honor of the king. George assembled a private library of sixty-five thousand volumes, which today forms the core of the British Library, and founded the Royal Academy of Arts in 1768 under Sir Joshua Reynolds. His greatest personal passion, however, was agriculture: he established model farms at Windsor, experimented with crop rotation, introduced Merino sheep to Britain, and contributed scholarly articles on farming under the pseudonym 'Ralph Robinson', earning the affectionate public moniker 'Farmer George'. George III's private life was a model of bourgeois diligence: he was an accomplished musician who played the flute and harpsichord, personally transcribing Handel's musical scores, and a discerning collector of architectural drawings and scientific clocks. His Royal Academy of Arts, chartered in 1768, launched the golden age of British portraiture and landscape painting under Reynolds and Gainsborough. At Windsor and Kew, 'Farmer George' was frequently seen walking across fields in muddy boots, talking amiably with local shepherds about sheep dip, soil drainage, and crop rotation, earning the genuine affection of rural Britons who saw in their sovereign the finest virtues of the English country gentleman.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SPARK OF REBELLION: THE STAMP ACT TO THE BOSTON TEA PARTY: 1765 TO 1773
The territorial triumph of the Seven Years' War left Great Britain with an astronomical national debt of one hundred and thirty-three million pounds. British ministers and King George believed it was only equitable that American colonists, whose defense against the French had cost British blood and treasure, should contribute to the costs of their own military garrisoning. In 1765, Parliament passed the Stamp Act, taxing legal documents and newspapers. The American colonies erupted in fury under the rallying cry: 'No taxation without representation!' Though Parliament repealed the Stamp Act, it asserted its absolute right to bind the colonies in all cases whatsoever in the Declaratory Act of 1766, following with the Townshend Duties on glass, lead, and tea. In December 1773, when the Sons of Liberty disguised as Mohawk Indians dumped three hundred and forty-two chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor, King George's patience broke. The King backed the punitive Coercive Acts—the 'Intolerable Acts'—closing Boston Harbor and placing Massachusetts under military rule, firmly declaring: 'The die is now cast; the colonies must either submit or triumph.' The dispute over parliamentary taxation in America was rooted in fundamentally incompatible constitutional philosophies. For King George and British parliamentarians, Parliament was the supreme, indivisible sovereign authority of the entire British Empire: if Parliament could not tax the colonies, imperial sovereignty was an illusion. For American colonists like Samuel Adams and Patrick Henry, taxation without representation violated the fundamental rights of Englishmen established by the 1689 Bill of Rights. When the Boston Tea Party dumped forty-six tons of tea into the harbor, George viewed the act as lawless vandalism that demanded military chastisement, firmly believing that leniency would unravel the entire imperial fabric.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE: JULY 1776
In April 1775, the first shots of the American Revolutionary War were fired at Lexington and Concord. In July 1775, the Continental Congress sent King George the 'Olive Branch Petition', pleading for reconciliation while blaming corrupt parliamentary ministers. George flatly refused to receive the petition, issuing a royal Proclamation of Rebellion declaring the colonists in open, armed rebellion and outside the King's protection, hiring twenty thousand German Hessian mercenaries to suppress the insurrection. This pushed the American colonies over the brink: in July 1776, Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence. Rather than attacking Parliament, the Declaration directed twenty-seven blistering indictments directly against King George III himself, branding him 'a Prince whose character is thus marked by every act which may define a Tyrant... unfit to be the ruler of a free people.' In New York City, ecstatic American soldiers pulled down the giant lead equestrian statue of King George at Bowling Green, melting it into forty-two thousand musket balls to fire at British troops. The hiring of thirty thousand German auxiliary troops—the 'Hessians'—by King George was a fateful strategic decision that inflamed American public opinion. American colonists viewed the introduction of foreign mercenaries as proof that their king was treating them not as rebellious subjects to be reconciled, but as foreign enemies to be slaughtered. In Philadelphia, Thomas Jefferson's fiery words in the Declaration of Independence permanently cast King George as the ultimate villain of the American Republic, blaming the monarch for inciting slave insurrections and native warfare, forging an enduring American myth of George III as a cruel, bloodthirsty tyrant.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: SARATOGA, YORKTOWN, AND THE LOSS OF AMERICA: 1777 TO 1781
Throughout the grueling war, King George was the fiercest, most unyielding hawk in the British Empire, constantly urging his ministers and generals—Lord North, William Howe, and Lord George Germain—to press the offensive. When British General John Burgoyne surrendered six thousand men at Saratoga in October 1777, France entered the war as an American ally, followed by Spain and the Dutch Republic, transforming the colonial rebellion into a global war for British imperial survival. The catastrophic climax came in October 1781 at Yorktown, Virginia: cornered on a peninsula by George Washington's army and Admiral de Grasse's French fleet, Lord Cornwallis surrendered eight thousand British soldiers. When Lord North received the catastrophic news in London, he threw up his arms, shouting: 'Oh God, it is all over!' King George drafted an abdication speech to Parliament, declaring he would return to Hanover rather than preside over the dismemberment of the Empire, before being persuaded by his ministers to accept reality. The Battle of Saratoga in October 1777 was the catastrophic turning point of the war: General Burgoyne's surrender brought French military forces under Rochambeau and naval fleets under de Grasse into the conflict, turning the American war into an unwinnable quagmire for Britain. At Yorktown in 1781, as British troops marched out to lay down their muskets, their military band famously played the melancholy ballad 'The World Turned Upside Down'. King George was so devastated by the defeat that he spent days drafting a formal letter of abdication to Parliament, resolving to retire to his ancestral electorate of Hanover rather than sign away his American empire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PEACE OF PARIS AND JOHN ADAMS: 1783 TO 1785
In September 1783, Great Britain signed the Treaty of Paris, formally recognizing the United States of America as a free, sovereign, and independent nation. For King George, the loss of America was an agonizing personal trauma that wounded his pride deeply. Yet when John Adams arrived at St. James's Palace in June 1785 as the first American Minister to the Court of St. James's, George handled the historic diplomatic encounter with magnificent, royal magnanimity. When Adams bowed and expressed his nation's desire for friendship, King George replied with emotional sincerity: 'I was the last to consent to the separation; but the separation having been made and having become inevitable, I have always said, as I say now, that I would be the first to meet the friendship of the United States as an independent power.' Adams was deeply moved, recording in his diary that the King had spoken with an honest dignity that honored both nations. When John Adams met King George III at St. James's Palace in June 1785, both men were visibly trembling with emotion. Adams delivered a dignified, formal address expressing the hope that the ancient friendship between the two nations might be restored. King George's reply was magnificent in its honesty: he acknowledged that he had fought to preserve his empire, but that he wished the new American republic every prosperity, wittily asking Adams if he had come from France, remarking: 'There is an opinion among some people that you are not the most attached of all your countrymen to the manners of France.' Adams cleverly replied that he had no attachment but to his own country, to which the King graciously said: 'An honest man will never have any other.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BOY PRIME MINISTER: WILLIAM PITT THE YOUNGER: 1783
In December 1783, following the collapse of the cynical Fox-North coalition, King George made an audacious, revolutionary appointment: he appointed twenty-four-year-old William Pitt the Younger as Prime Minister. Opposition MPs burst into mocking laughter, ridiculing the government as a 'mince-pie administration' that would not survive the Christmas holidays. But Pitt was an administrative genius of ice-cold intellect, integrity, and eloquence. In the general election of 1784, the British electorate rallied behind the young Prime Minister and the King, giving Pitt a massive parliamentary majority. Over the next decade, Pitt reformed British finances, created the Sinking Fund to reduce national debt, clamped down on smuggling, and forged a harmonious working partnership with King George III. Britain stabilized, its economy flourished, and the nation regained its global prestige, preparing Great Britain to face the cataclysmic storm of the French Revolution. William Pitt the Younger's appointment as Prime Minister in December 1783 was the political masterstroke of George III's reign. At just twenty-four, Pitt possessed an austere, unshakeable integrity that restored national confidence after the humilating loss of America. Together, King George and Pitt established a stable governing coalition that modernized the British economy, expanded trade with India and China, and reformed the Royal Navy, laying the essential fiscal and military foundations that would enable Great Britain to withstand the colossal storm of the Napoleonic Wars.

[Rebecca - Host]
